extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in political economy — students, informed citizens, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: An essay-style exposition on the nature and proper limits of government, taxation, and money — critiquing popular illusions and utopian policy proposals and emphasizing economic principles. Intended as a polemical/educational preface in political economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Government as reciprocal plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: "Government is the great fiction, through which everybody endeavours to live at the expense of everybody else."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the mechanism by which individuals who wish to profit from others appeal to the Government to make such appropriation lawful and easy; emphasizes that officials, like other men, seize opportunities to increase wealth and influence, producing 'reciprocal plunder.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative role of Government: organized common force
rubrics_metrics.description: "Government is and ought to be nothing whatever but common force organized, not to be an instrument of oppression and mutual plunder among citizens; but, on the contrary, to secure to every one his own, and to cause justice and security to reign."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive standard: government should be limited to protecting property, justice, and security rather than acting as benefactor or redistributor; policy should avoid turning government into an engine of mutual appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility constraint: cannot promise many benefits and no taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The public expects "many benefits and no taxes"; such contradictory promises are impossible to realize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and evaluate government programmes by checking resource feasibility: promises of extensive services without corresponding revenue are self-contradictory and will lead to either new taxes, broken promises, or fiscal collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional phrasing shapes public expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Personifying Government in constitutional language (as in the French example) encourages citizens to expect benefits from a separate abstract being; by contrast, the US preamble emphasizes citizens' responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or interpreting constitutional/political texts, prefer formulations that attribute responsibility to the people rather than implying an independent beneficent entity; assess how phrasing influences public demands and political culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government's twin hands: taking (rough) and giving (smooth) — redistribution has costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Government has two hands — one to receive and the other to give; the activity of the giving hand is subordinate to the taking hand and it is "radically impossible" for government to restore more than it has taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate redistributive policies by accounting for the administrative and incentive costs of collection and distribution; recognize that appropriation and redistribution necessarily diminish net public welfare by at least the cost of the 'expensive medium' called government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legality does not alter economic/moral effects of plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: "Reciprocal plunder is no less plunder because it is reciprocal; that it is no less criminal because it is executed legally and with order; that it adds nothing to the public good..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing policy outcomes, do not assume legality or procedural regularity implies positive public value; evaluate the substantive transfer effects and net social cost regardless of legal sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Populist/utopian promises produce instability and revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambitious promises (work, bread, assistance, colonies, free instruction, low taxes) that cannot be fulfilled lead to popular disillusionment, revolutions, and cycles of governments making unrealistic pledges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge political platforms and government manifestos for internal consistency and resource realism; detect promises that are strategically useful for popularity but structurally impossible, as they signal likely future instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal sustainability: short-term credit postpones harm and causes bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: "To live upon credit, which is the same as exhausting the future, is certainly a present means of reconciling [contradictory promises] ... but such proceedings call forth the spectre of bankruptcy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluation must include intertemporal accounting: avoid treating current credit-financed benefits as equivalent to sustainably funded policies; consider long-term insolvency and the political consequences of debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-funding alignment: services require adequate revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of services Governments are said to be 'bound' to provide (education, assistance to aged, regulation of credit, purchase of railroads/canals/mines, etc.) must be matched with resources; philanthropy without exchequer is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or appraising public programs, require explicit, realistic revenue sources; beware of proposals that expand obligations while proposing to abolish main tax bases (salt, stamps, customs, patents, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish money from wealth: wealth arises from labour and exchange, not cash
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth is labour and exchange; money is a medium. Confusing cash with real wealth leads to errors and damaging policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic policy and discourse should prioritize production, exchange, and real goods/services as the basis of prosperity rather than measures of money supply alone; critique policies built on the assumption that more cash equals more wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-mercantilist principle: hoarding cash/prohibiting imports is self-defeating
rubrics_metrics.description: An absolute-king thought experiment shows that forbidding exports of specie and prohibiting imports or forcing exports leads to retaliation, war, and ultimately failure to increase national wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject zero-sum mercantilist policies that aim to 'increase the heap of money' by restricting trade; favour policies that enable exchange and recognize mutual gains from trade to avoid conflict and economic ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy realism: account for human incentives and needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative experiments that ignore hunger, self-interest, and human incentives (e.g., forbidding export of money or abolishing money) will fail because people act according to their needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess policy proposals for behavioral plausibility; require mechanisms robust to predictable human responses rather than assuming ideal compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax-base realism: taxing only 'superfluities' is naive
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to abolish taxes on necessities (salt, liquors, letters, etc.) while preserving funds by taxing 'superfluities' overlook practical realities and will likely lead to heavier burdens elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating tax reform, scrutinize the practical incidence and sufficiency of proposed bases; ensure redistribution of tax burdens does not merely shift or intensify costs on taxpayers in disguise.
